title: Diversity as Insurance: Genotype-Rich Outplanting at Morrow Cays
artefact:
# Diversity as Insurance: Genotype-Rich Outplanting at Morrow Cays

## Summary

A common restoration question is whether limited nursery stock should be spread across many coral genotypes or concentrated in a few proven performers. We examined 5,408 *Acropora cervicornis* fragments planted in paired four-genotype and twelve-genotype plots at Morrow Cays. After 20 months, including one heat pulse and one period of heavy swell, twelve-genotype plots had 7.1 percentage points higher adjusted survival than four-genotype plots. They also had substantially less variation in mortality through time, while growth among surviving colonies was similar.

The advantage did not appear before environmental stress. It emerged because mortality was less synchronized among genotypes in diverse plots: losses in susceptible genotypes were partly offset by stable performance elsewhere in the portfolio. The evidence supports genotype-rich planting as a risk-management strategy, but it does not establish twelve as an optimal number or show that the benefit will persist through multiple severe disturbances.

## Data and design

The Morrow Cays restoration team established 52 plots between February 2023 and April 2023. Each of 26 reef blocks contained one four-genotype plot and one twelve-genotype plot, separated by 18–35 metres. All plots began with 104 fragments at the same nominal spacing.

Four-genotype plots contained 26 fragments per genotype. Twelve-genotype plots contained eight or nine fragments per genotype. Genotypes were drawn from a nursery catalogue of 31 lineages, and 19 lineages appeared in both treatments. Initial effective richness, calculated from genotype proportions, averaged 3.7 in the four-genotype plots and 9.8 in the twelve-genotype plots.

Divers were intended to alternate treatment placement within blocks, but allocation was not formally randomized. Baseline depth, rugosity, fragment size and benthic cover were nevertheless similar between treatments. Twelve-genotype plots were 0.3 metres deeper on average, and this difference was included in adjusted models.

Colonies were assessed at planting and after 3, 6, 9, 12, 16 and 20 months. Image reviewers, who did not receive treatment labels, recorded survival, live-tissue length and detachment. Temperature loggers documented an 18-day heat pulse between months 10 and 12. Unusually heavy swell occurred shortly before the month-16 survey.

Of 32,448 scheduled fragment-level observations, 3.7% could not be scored because images were absent or obstructed. The primary analysis treated these observations as missing until the fragment was seen again; fragments missing at the final survey were excluded from the corresponding survival estimate.

## Analysis

We fitted a discrete-time survival model with a complementary log-log link. Fixed terms included richness treatment, survey interval, treatment-by-interval interaction, depth, starting fragment length and local macroalgal cover. Reef block was included as a fixed effect, while plot and nursery genotype were crossed random intercepts. Adjusted cumulative survival was standardized to the full sample’s baseline covariate distribution.

Temporal instability was measured as the within-plot standard deviation of monthly mortality hazard across the six intervals. Because two intervals lasted four rather than three months, interval losses were converted to monthly hazards before comparison. Confidence intervals for instability and synchrony metrics came from 2,000 bootstrap samples drawn at the reef-block level.

To examine the proposed mechanism, we estimated correlations among genotype-specific mortality deviations after removing block and interval averages. Twelve-genotype plots were repeatedly rarefied to four genotypes so that their correlation estimates were not mechanically more stable merely because they contained more lineages.

## Results

| Outcome | Four genotypes | Twelve genotypes | Adjusted contrast |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Survival before heat pulse, month 9 | 90.1% | 91.0% | +1.2 pp (95% CI: −1.8 to +4.0) |
| Survival after heat pulse, month 12 | 71.4% | 79.2% | +7.6 pp (+2.3 to +12.8) |
| Survival at month 20 | 62.3% | 69.8% | +7.1 pp (+1.0 to +13.1) |
| SD of monthly mortality hazard | 0.108 | 0.074 | Ratio 0.69 (0.54 to 0.89) |
| Live-tissue growth among survivors | 22.4 cm | 21.6 cm | −0.8 cm (−3.4 to +1.9) |

Survival trajectories were nearly indistinguishable through month 9. The largest treatment separation occurred during the heat-pulse interval, when adjusted mortality was 20.8% in four-genotype plots and 13.1% in twelve-genotype plots. The gap narrowed slightly after the swell event but remained evident at month 20.

The estimated richness effect varied meaningfully among blocks. Twelve-genotype plots outperformed their paired four-genotype plots in 18 of 26 blocks, showed little difference in five, and performed worse in three. Two of the three reversals occurred on the shallowest reef shelf, where detachment rather than tissue loss dominated mortality.

Rarefied mean pairwise correlation in genotype mortality was 0.41 in four-genotype plots and 0.26 in twelve-genotype plots, a difference of −0.15 (bootstrap 95% CI: −0.27 to −0.03). This lower synchrony is consistent with a portfolio effect: diverse plots did not avoid stress, but fewer of their component genotypes declined at the same time.

There was no detectable growth benefit among survivors. In addition, the four nursery lineages with the highest individual survival were present in both treatment groups. Excluding those lineages reduced overall survival but left the richness contrast similar, indicating that the result was not driven solely by placing one exceptional lineage in diverse plots.

## Robustness checks

Three alternative treatments of missing observations produced month-20 richness advantages ranging from 5.9 to 7.8 percentage points. Counting every final missing observation as dead yielded the smallest estimate. Excluding the two shallowest blocks produced an adjusted difference of 7.5 percentage points. A continuous model using effective richness rather than the assigned treatment estimated a 0.9-percentage-point increase in month-20 survival per additional effective genotype, although the relationship flattened above approximately nine genotypes.

These checks support the direction of the result, but the apparent plateau should not be treated as a threshold. Few plots occupied the middle of the richness range, so the data primarily distinguish two planting strategies rather than map a complete dose-response curve.

## Interpretation and operational implications

The principal value of genotype richness at Morrow Cays was stability, not faster growth or uniformly higher performance. Concentrating fragments in a few historically successful lineages would have looked efficient during the first nine months, yet it would have increased exposure to synchronized loss during the heat pulse.

For the next planting cycle, a reasonable operational target is at least nine effectively represented genotypes per plot, with no single genotype comprising more than 15% of fragments. This recommendation should be applied as a diversification rule rather than as evidence that nine is biologically optimal. Managers should also retain replication across reef blocks; genotype diversity did not eliminate losses associated with shallow, high-energy habitat.

The inference has three important limits. First, treatment placement was paired but not randomized, so unmeasured microhabitat differences could account for part of the survival gap. Second, 20 months and one documented heat pulse are insufficient to establish long-term resilience. Third, nursery genotype labels were based on propagation records rather than genomic verification, leaving some possibility of duplicate or misassigned lineages. Continued monitoring and genetic confirmation would clarify whether the observed insurance effect persists and how much true diversity is required.

Indeed, the gap narrowed after the swell, and treatment performance varied among blocks. The report acknowledges this limitation, but the title, risk-management framing, and planting guidance still invite broader application than one event history can validate. valid.basis: Nursery genotype labels lacked genomic confirmation, which may bias both effective-richness assignments and the genotype-level synchrony mechanism.
valid.message: A further deduction is warranted because the key explanatory variable was not independently verified. “Genotypes” came from nursery propagation records rather than genomic confirmation, so duplicate clones could be counted as distinct lineages and misassigned fragments could contaminate both treatments. Consequently, the portfolio-effect mechanism is less secure than the survival contrast itself. The authors disclose the issue, but a study centered on genotypic insurance needs stronger identity validation to merit an exceptional score. valid.message: The score should rise because the quantitative execution is unusually complete for an applied field study. Uncertainty for the stability and synchrony outcomes is bootstrapped at the reef-block level rather than treating fragments as independent. Missing observations are addressed through three alternative assumptions, and exclusions and continuous-richness specifications preserve the result’s direction. Crucially, twelve-genotype plots are rarefied to four genotypes, reducing the risk that their lower estimated correlation merely reflects having more lineages available for calculation.
